text: From late July 2001, people in parts of [[@kerala|Kerala]], especially Kottayam and Idukki districts, saw red rain falling. It came in short showers, on and off, for about two months. Clothes hung out to dry turned pink. Some people also reported yellow, green and black rain.

The Centre for Earth Science Studies in Thiruvananthapuram and the Tropical Botanic Garden and Research Institute investigated. They found the red colour came from tiny spores of an [[algae|alga]] called *Trentepohlia*, which grows on trees, rocks and walls across Kerala. Why so many spores got into the rain at once is still not fully understood. But the cause of the colour has been identified.

st.prompt: What made the rain in Kerala red in 2001?

options.t: Tiny spores from a kind of alga
Red desert dust from Arabia
Iron dust from a meteor

st.reveal: A government study found the red colour came from spores of an alga called Trentepohlia, common in Kerala. Scientists still argue about exactly how so many spores got into the rain at once, but the spores themselves have been identified.

n.certNote: Most scientists accept the Indian government study that found the red colour came from spores of a common alga. A few researchers argued for other causes, including from space, but those claims have not been accepted.

sec.t:
The first red rain fell on 25 July 2001. Showers were often local, falling over a few square kilometres and lasting only minutes. Many people collected samples in bottles. Under a [[microscope|microscope]], the red water was full of tiny round particles, each about a hundredth of a millimetre across.

People were worried. Some thought it was blood, or a sign. Others feared chemical pollution. Newspapers carried rumours. The government asked scientists to investigate quickly. Samples were collected from dozens of places, and some were kept in fridges and studied for years afterwards.

Scientists at the Tropical Botanic Garden grew the particles in the lab. They became an alga, *Trentepohlia annulata*, which lives on land. It is a relative of green seaweeds, but it has an orange-red colour, from the same family of [[pigment|pigments]] that makes carrots orange.

In Kerala's wet [[@monsoon|monsoon]], *Trentepohlia* grows thickly on tree trunks, rocks and even lamp posts in the area where red rain fell. When it releases spores, they can be carried into the air. Scientists think heavy rain washed huge numbers of spores out of the sky at once. Some researchers have suggested that unusual winds or weather in 2001 helped lift many spores into the clouds. That part is still debated.

In 2006, two physicists from Mahatma Gandhi University in Kottayam, Godfrey Louis and A. Santhosh Kumar, published a paper suggesting the red cells could have come from space, perhaps from a [[comet|comet]]. They said the cells did not contain DNA, which would make them very strange.

Other scientists were not convinced. The alga had already been grown from the samples in a lab, which pointed firmly to a living thing from Earth. Most researchers accept the algae explanation. The space idea remains a reminder that big claims need big evidence.

Red rain has been reported in Kerala again, including in 2012, and in other places around the world, such as Sri Lanka in 2012. Coloured rain can also be caused by dust. Red rain sometimes falls in Europe when strong winds carry Sahara desert dust north. In India, dust storms can tint rain in the north.

So coloured rain isn't magic. It is rain that has picked up something on the way down: dust, spores or pollution. For stranger rain still, look beyond Earth. On some distant planets, scientists think it may [[@space-weird-rain|rain glass or even metal]], sideways, at thousands of kilometres an hour.

text: The Milky Way is our [[galaxy|galaxy]]: a huge, flat, spinning disc of stars, gas and dust, held together by [[gravity|gravity]]. The Sun is one of somewhere between 100 billion and 400 billion stars in it.

On a dark night, away from city lights, you can see part of the disc as a faint, glowing band across the sky. That band is the light of countless distant stars, too far away to see one by one. Ancient Greeks thought it looked like spilled milk. In [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] and Hindi it is called Akash Ganga, the river of the sky.

st.prompt: The Sun is carrying us around the centre of the Milky Way. How long does one full lap take?

options.t: About 230 million years
One year
About 10,000 years

st.reveal: About 230 million years, even though we are moving at around 800,000 km/h. The last time the Sun was where it is now, the very first dinosaurs were only just appearing.

n.certNote: Because we are inside the Milky Way, it is hard to measure. Estimates of how many stars it holds range from about 100 billion to 400 billion, and its width is still being refined.

d.try: Make a model galaxy. Draw a fat dot in the middle of a dark sheet of paper, then sprinkle a pinch of salt or sugar in two curving arms around it. Mark the Sun about two-thirds of the way out from the centre. Now look at it edge-on, at eye level. You see a thin band, just as we see the Milky Way across the sky.
myth: The Sun sits at the centre of the Milky Way.

Astronomers believed this until about a hundred years ago. In 1918, the American astronomer Harlow Shapley showed that we are far out in the disc, about halfway to the edge. The centre lies towards the constellation Sagittarius.
facts: Sagittarius A*, about 4 million times the Sun's mass

sec.t:
Seen from outside, the Milky Way would look like a giant pinwheel, with a bright bulge in the middle and curving arms of stars. A straight bar of stars crosses the centre, which is why [[astronomer|astronomers]] call it a barred spiral.

The galaxy is about 100,000 [[@light-years|light-years]] across. Light, the fastest thing there is, would take 100,000 years to cross it. If the whole Milky Way were shrunk to the width of India, the paths of [[@planets-order|all eight planets]] around the Sun would fit inside a bottle cap, about 3 cm wide.

We live in a quieter area about 26,000 [[lightyear|light-years]] from the centre. When you look at the Milky Way's band in the sky, you are looking along the flat disc from the inside.

That makes mapping it hard, like trying to draw a map of a forest while standing among the trees. Thick dust hides much of the disc. Astronomers use radio [[@telescopes-how|telescopes]] and [[infrared|infrared]] light, which pass through dust, to trace the spiral arms. The European Space Agency's Gaia spacecraft, launched in 2013, measured the positions of more than a billion stars to build the best map yet.

In 1610, [[@galileo|Galileo]] pointed one of the first telescopes at the Milky Way. He discovered it was made of huge numbers of faint stars packed together. Before that, nobody knew what the glow was.

Today most people can't see it at all. Streetlights and buildings light up the sky so much that the faint band disappears. In 2022, India set up its first [[@stargazing|dark-sky reserve]] at Hanle in [[@ladakh|Ladakh]], high in the mountains, where the Milky Way still stretches clearly from one horizon to the other.

The Milky Way is not alone. Two small galaxies, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, can be seen from the southern half of the world. The nearest big spiral galaxy, Andromeda, is about 2.5 million light-years away and moving towards us.

Astronomers have long expected the two to [[@galaxy-collisions|collide]] in about 4 to 5 billion years. Newer studies suggest it is far from certain. Even if they do meet, the stars are so far apart that they would almost never hit each other.

text: The North Star, also called Polaris, sits almost exactly above Earth's North Pole. As Earth spins, the whole sky seems to turn around that point. Stars far from it sweep across the sky in big arcs. Polaris is so close to the centre that it hardly moves at all.
Think of a spinning merry-go-round. A child on the edge whizzes round in a big circle. A child sitting right at the middle just turns on the spot. Polaris is the child at the middle.
In India it is known as Dhruva tara. In a well-known story from the Puranas, the boy Dhruva prayed so steadily that he was given a place in the sky as the star that never moves.

st.prompt: How high above the horizon do you see the North Star?

options.t: The same number of degrees as your latitude
Always straight overhead
It changes with the time of night

st.reveal: At the North Pole, latitude 90 degrees, Polaris is overhead. At the equator, latitude 0, it sits on the horizon. In Delhi, at about 29 degrees, it is about 29 degrees up. Sailors used this to work out how far north they were.

d.try: Open an old dark umbrella and stick small paper stars on the inside, with one right at the centre where the shaft meets the cloth. Hold it above your head and turn the handle slowly. Every star circles except the one in the middle.
myth: The North Star is the brightest star in the night sky.
Polaris is only moderately bright, around the 48th brightest. The brightest star at night is Sirius. Polaris is special because of where it is, not how bright it is.
facts: Polaris, or Dhruva tara in India
Distance from the sky's north pole

sec.t:
The stars don't really move across the sky each night. Earth turns once a day, which gives us [[@day-night|day and night]], and that makes the sky look as if it is turning the other way.

Earth spins around an imaginary line called its [[axis|axis]], which runs through the North and South Poles. Point that line out into space from the North Pole and it lands less than one degree from Polaris. So while everything else circles, Polaris stays put.

If you leave a camera pointed at the northern sky for a few hours, the stars draw bright circles in the photo. Polaris makes a tiny arc near the centre.

sec.h: A star for finding your way
sec.t:
Because Polaris always marks north, travellers have used it for centuries. Its height above the horizon tells you your [[@coordinates|latitude]]. Arab and Indian sailors crossing the Indian Ocean measured it with a kamal, a small wooden board on a knotted string. In Bengaluru, at about 13 degrees north, it sits low in the northern sky. In New York, at about 41 degrees, it is much higher. From Australia or South Africa you cannot see it at all, and there is no bright star marking the south pole of the sky.

Polaris shows true north, which is not quite where a compass points. A compass follows [[@earth-magnet|Earth's magnetic field]], whose north pole is in a different place.

In the United States before the Civil War, many people escaping slavery travelled by night towards the North Star, heading for free states and Canada. [[@harriet-tubman|Harriet Tubman]], who led dozens of people to freedom, is said to have used it to guide them.

{{story:harriet-tubman}}

Earth's axis is not fixed forever. Like a slowing [[@yo-yo-tops|spinning top]], it wobbles in a slow circle, taking about 26,000 years to go round once. As it does, it points at different stars.

When the [[@pyramids|pyramids of Giza]] were built, about 4,500 years ago, the pole star was Thuban, a faint star in the [[constellation|constellation]] Draco. Polaris is getting closer to the true pole and will be nearest around the year 2100. In about 12,000 years, the brilliant star Vega will be close enough to serve as the North Star.

Through a big telescope, Polaris turns out to be at least three stars travelling together. The main one is a [[@stars-colours|yellow-white supergiant]], far larger and brighter than our Sun. It looks faint only because it is a few hundred [[@light-years|light-years]] away. Its brightness also pulses very slightly every few days, which makes it useful to [[astronomer|astronomers]] measuring distances across space.

text: Yes, probably, if we see it coming early enough. In 2022, NASA's DART mission crashed a spacecraft into a small [[asteroid|asteroid]] called Dimorphos on purpose. The hit changed its [[orbit|orbit]], proving for the first time that humans can move a natural object in space.

The real challenge is finding dangerous asteroids years or decades before they arrive. A small push far in advance is all it takes to turn a hit into a miss. Telescopes around the world now track more than 40,000 near-Earth asteroids, and none of the known large ones is set to hit us in the next century.

st.prompt: How did DART change the path of the asteroid it hit?

options.t: By smashing into it and knocking it slightly off course
By blowing it up with explosives
By towing it with a long cable

st.reveal: DART simply crashed into Dimorphos at about 22,000 km/h. The hit, plus the huge spray of rock it blasted into space, gave the asteroid a small push. That was enough to make its orbit around its bigger partner 32 minutes shorter.

src: NASA, Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission results.
European Space Agency, Planetary Defence Office and Hera mission.
n.certNote: The DART test proved that hitting an asteroid can nudge it. Whether we could stop a large asteroid in time depends on how early we spot it, and some methods have never been tested.

d.try: Roll a big ball slowly across the floor and try to make it miss a target, like a shoe, by tapping it with a small ball. Try tapping it early in its roll, then late. You will find a tiny tap early works better than a hard hit at the last moment. That is the key idea of asteroid defence.
myth: The best way to stop an asteroid is to blow it into pieces with a nuclear bomb, like in the films.

Breaking an asteroid apart could send many big chunks towards Earth. Scientists prefer to nudge it gently, years ahead, so it misses. Nuclear devices are studied only as a last resort, mainly to push an asteroid rather than shatter it.

sec.h: The car that hit an asteroid

sec.t: The European Space Agency launched a spacecraft called Hera in 2024 to inspect the scene. It is due to reach Didymos and Dimorphos in late 2026. Hera will measure the [[crater|crater]], the asteroid's mass and its shape, to work out exactly how well the push worked. That will help engineers plan a real rescue mission if one is ever needed.

Small space rocks hit Earth all the time, mostly burning up harmlessly as shooting stars. Bigger ones are rarer. In February 2013, a rock about 18 m wide exploded over the Russian city of Chelyabinsk. The shock wave shattered windows across the city and injured around 1,500 people, mostly from flying glass. Nobody had seen it coming, because it approached from the direction of the Sun.

In 1908, a larger object exploded over Tunguska in Siberia and flattened about 80 million trees across 2,000 km². And 66 million years ago, an asteroid about 10 km wide helped end the age of the dinosaurs, though scientists still argue about how much giant volcanoes added to [[@dino-extinction-theories|the dinosaurs' extinction]].

In December 2024, [[astronomer|astronomers]] found an asteroid about 40 to 90 m across, named 2024 YR4. By February 2025, its chance of hitting Earth in December 2032 had climbed to about 3 percent. Space agencies began planning. Then new [[@telescopes-how|telescope]] observations pinned down its path, and the chance of hitting Earth fell to almost zero.

For a while it still had a small chance, about 4 percent in mid-2025, of hitting the Moon in 2032. Then, in 2026, new observations by the James Webb Space Telescope ruled out a Moon hit too.

Hitting an asteroid isn't the only idea. A "[[gravity|gravity]] tractor" would fly a heavy spacecraft alongside an asteroid for years, using the spacecraft's tiny gravity to slowly tug it. Lasers or mirrors focusing sunlight could boil rock off one side, pushing it like a slow rocket. For a huge asteroid found late, a nuclear device exploded nearby might be the last option.

All of these work better the earlier they start. That is why NASA is building NEO Surveyor, a space telescope due to launch around 2027, to hunt asteroids in [[infrared|infrared]] light.

On 13 April 2029, an asteroid called Apophis, about 340 m wide, will pass about 32,000 km from Earth, closer than the satellites that beam TV signals. It will be visible to the naked eye from parts of the world. Scientists are sure it will miss. Space agencies, including ESA and ISRO, have discussed sending spacecraft to study it during the visit. Knowing exactly where a rock like that will be in 20 years is a puzzle of [[@probability|probability]] as much as rockets.

text: Most crew spacecraft are built in two halves. On top sits the crew module, the capsule where astronauts ride. Below it is the service module, which holds the engines, fuel tanks and power systems.

Before coming home, the two halves must part. Only the capsule returns to Earth. To split them, engineers use small, carefully timed explosive devices, called pyrotechnics, that cut the links between them in a fraction of a second.

quiz.prompt: Why does only the crew module come back to Earth, and not the whole spacecraft?

options.t: Only the crew module has a heat shield to survive the fiery trip through the air
The service module is needed to stay in space as a space station
The service module is too light to fall back down

quiz.reveal: Coming home from space, a spacecraft slams into the air so fast that it gets hotter than a furnace. Only the crew module has a thick heat shield on its base. Carrying the service module along would add weight with no protection, so it is let go and burns up high in the sky.

d.try: Snap two LEGO bricks together, then try to pull them apart with one quick, clean tug so neither wobbles. It is harder than it looks. Engineers have to make sure a spacecraft's two halves part just as cleanly, every single time.
myth: Spacecraft come back to Earth in one piece, just like they went up.
Most spacecraft drop parts on the way. Rockets shed stages going up, and capsules leave their service module behind before coming down. Only a small part actually lands.

sec.t:
The two halves are joined by bolts, clamps and umbilical lines, the cables and pipes that carry electricity and fluids between them. At the moment of separation, every one of these must be cut at once. If one link holds on, the capsule could tumble.

The cut also sends a sharp jolt and shaking, or [[vibration|vibration]], through the capsule. So engineers test it on the ground first, in a rig covered in [[sensor|sensors]], and check that computers, [[navigation|navigation]] equipment and the heat shield all come through unharmed. In October 2026, ISRO ran exactly these tests for [[@gaganyaan|Gaganyaan]], India's spacecraft for carrying people.

New crew spacecraft usually fly without people first. For Gaganyaan's first flight, a human-shaped [[@tech-robots-space|robot]] called Vyommitra was chosen to ride in the capsule and report back on what astronauts would feel.

Engineers also drop capsules from aircraft to test their parachutes, and practise turning a capsule upright after it lands in the water. Each test removes one more risk before [[@indian-astronauts|astronauts]] climb aboard.

text: A honeybee that finds flowers comes home and does a "waggle dance" on the honeycomb.
The direction of the waggle shows the direction of the flowers compared with the Sun. The length of the waggle shows how far.
Karl von Frisch figured this out and won a Nobel Prize in 1973. He shared it with two other scientists who studied animal behaviour.

quiz.prompt: Inside the dark hive, a bee waggles straight up the honeycomb. Where is the food?

options.t: Straight towards the Sun
Straight up in the sky
Directly away from the Sun

quiz.reveal: On the upright comb, "straight up" stands for the direction of the Sun. A waggle straight up means "fly towards the Sun". A waggle pointing a little to the right of straight up means "fly a little to the right of the Sun", and so on.

src: von Frisch K. (1967) The Dance Language and Orientation of Bees. Harvard University Press.

d.try: Play the bee dance game. Hide a small object somewhere in a room or playground. Then, without words or pointing, show a friend where it is. Walk in a straight line facing the direction they should go, and wiggle for longer if it's far away. Can they find it from your dance alone?
myth: Every bee in the hive is busy collecting nectar from flowers.

Only the older worker bees go out to gather food. Younger workers clean cells, feed the young, build comb and guard the entrance. The queen lays eggs, and male bees, called drones, don't collect food at all.

giant rock bee, Asian hive bee, dwarf honeybee

sec.t:
The dancer runs in a short straight line, shaking her body from side to side very fast. Then she loops back round to the start, first to the right, then to the left, tracing a figure of eight. Other bees crowd around her in the dark, feeling her movements with their antennae.

The straight "waggle run" is the message. Inside the hive, the comb hangs upright. Straight up stands for the direction of the Sun. If the flowers are 40 degrees to the left of the Sun, she waggles 40 degrees to the left of straight up. The longer the waggle lasts, the further away the food. In many hives, a waggle of about one second means roughly a kilometre of flying, though each colony's "[[@dialects|dialect]]" is a little different.

She also carries the scent of the flowers on her body, and shares tastes of the [[nectar|nectar]]. So the recruits know what to look for and what it smells like.

{{story:sun-what}}

sec.h: A scientist with a box of bees
sec.t:
Karl von Frisch began studying bees in Austria in the early 1900s. He trained them to visit dishes of sugar water, marked each bee with a dot of paint, and watched through glass-sided hives. He noticed that when one bee found a rich dish, her nestmates soon arrived even if he moved it far away.

Over many years of patient experiments, he showed that the dance carried both direction and distance. Many scientists at first doubted that an insect could share such detailed information. Later researchers built a tiny [[@robots|robot]] bee that danced in a hive. Many real bees followed its dance and searched in the right direction and at the right distance.

India is home to several wild honeybee [[species|species]]. Three are especially common. The giant rock bee builds a single huge comb in the open, hanging from cliffs, tall trees and buildings. With no walls, its dancers perform right on the comb's surface in daylight, on the curtain of bees.

The Asian hive bee nests in hollow trees and walls and is kept in wooden boxes by beekeepers. The tiny dwarf honeybee builds a palm-sized comb wrapped around a twig. It dances on the flat top of its comb, pointing straight at the food, without needing to turn the Sun into "up".

Dancing isn't only for flowers. When a colony grows too big, half the bees leave with the old queen and hang in a cluster on a branch. Scout bees fly off to inspect possible homes, then dance to describe them. The better the site, the more energetically they dance.

The American scientist Thomas Seeley spent years watching these swarms. He found that scouts gradually come to agree as weak sites lose dancers. When enough scouts are dancing for one site, the whole swarm takes off together. A cloud of insects makes a group decision without any leader.

Bees pollinate many of the fruits, vegetables and nuts we eat, from mangoes and apples to almonds and mustard. Some plants, like [[@fig-wasps|figs]], rely on other insects instead. Each worker visits many flowers on a single trip, her wings [[@insect-flight|beating]] over 200 times a second, collecting nectar to make [[@honey|honey]] and carrying [[pollen|pollen]] from bloom to bloom. Their dance helps the colony send its workers to the best flowers quickly, wasting as little flying as possible. To store all that honey, they build wax cells in a near-perfect [[@honeycomb|hexagon]] pattern.

text: Looking after a pet means giving it everything it would find for itself in the wild, and a bit more. Every pet needs the right food, clean water, a safe and comfortable place to live, and [[@jobs-vet|a vet]] when it is sick. Most also need exercise, things to explore and company, whether from people or other animals.

Different pets need very different things. A dog needs daily walks and training. A cat needs places to climb and scratch. Fish need clean, filtered water at the right temperature. Before getting any pet, a family should find out how big it will grow, how long it will live and how much care it will need.

st.reveal: Chocolate contains a substance called theobromine that dogs break down very slowly, so it builds up and can make them seriously ill. Dark chocolate is the most dangerous. Grapes, raisins, onions and garlic are also unsafe for dogs.

myth: Goldfish have a memory of only three seconds.

Experiments have shown that goldfish can learn tasks, such as pushing a lever for food, and remember them for weeks or months. A goldfish in a bare little bowl still needs a proper tank, clean water and space to swim.

sec.t:
People and animals have lived together for a very long time. [[@dogs-domestic|Dogs]] were the first animals to be [[domesticate|domesticated]], [[@wolves-india|descended from wolves]] at least 15,000 years ago, though estimates vary. They helped people hunt, guard camps and herd animals.

[[@cats-domestic|Cats]] probably moved in later, when farming began and grain stores attracted mice. In 2004, [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] reported a grave in Cyprus where a person was buried with a cat about 9,500 years ago. In [[@ancient-egypt|ancient Egypt]], cats were so loved that some were mummified. Today, roughly two-thirds of households in the United States have a pet, according to a 2023 industry survey, and [[@life-pets-world|pet-keeping]] is growing fast in Indian cities.

Pets should visit a vet for check-ups and [[@vaccines|vaccines]]. In India, rabies is a serious danger. The World Health Organization says India has a large share of the world's rabies deaths, mostly from dog bites, and vaccinating pet dogs and cats helps protect both animals and people.

Children should also learn to read animals' moods. Never disturb a dog that is eating or sleeping, and always ask the owner before stroking an unfamiliar pet. If an animal ever bites or scratches you, tell a grown-up straight away, so the wound can be cleaned and checked by a doctor.

Some animals are not meant to be pets. In India, native wild birds such as rose-ringed parakeets and munias are protected under the Wildlife Protection Act, and keeping them in cages is against the law. Turtles, [[@turtles-tortoises|star tortoises]] and monkeys are often sold illegally too.

Indian street dogs, often called Indies, can make loyal, healthy pets and are well suited to the [[climate|climate]]. Many families adopt dogs and cats from animal shelters instead of buying them. Whatever the pet, caring for it well is a long promise. Some cats and dogs live for 15 years or more, and some parrots and tortoises can outlive their owners.

text: Ballet began about 500 years ago as entertainment in the royal courts of Italy, during the [[@renaissance|Renaissance]]. Rich families put on grand shows with music, poetry, costumes and dancing at weddings and feasts. When the Italian noblewoman Catherine de' Medici married into the French royal family, she helped bring these spectacles to France.

In France, ballet became a serious art with strict rules. King Louis XIV, who loved to dance, founded a royal dance academy in 1661. Teachers there set down the basic positions and steps, with French names still used everywhere today. Later, ballet grew in [[@russia|Russia]], where famous works such as *Swan Lake* and *The Nutcracker* were created, and then spread around the world.

d.try: Hold the back of a chair for balance and stand with your heels together and toes pointing outwards, as far as is comfortable. That is first position. Slowly bend your knees over your toes, keeping your back straight, then straighten up. You have just done a plié, the first exercise in almost every ballet class.
myth: Ballet is only for girls.

Ballet began with men. Kings and noblemen danced in the earliest court ballets, and many famous ballet stars, choreographers and teachers have been men. Ballet training demands huge strength from every dancer.

sec.t:
Over time, professional dancers replaced nobles, and ballet moved from palace halls to public theatres in [[@paris|Paris]] and elsewhere. Skirts became shorter so audiences could see the feet. Dancers began to jump higher and spin faster.

In the early 1800s, ballerinas started dancing on the very tips of their toes, called dancing *en pointe*. In 1832, the Italian-Swedish ballerina Marie Taglioni danced *La Sylphide* in Paris, floating on her toes as a fairy spirit. It made her a star. Pointe shoes have a stiff box at the toe, built from layers of fabric, paper and glue, and a firm sole for support.

In the 1800s, the Russian tsars spent fortunes on ballet. A French choreographer, Marius Petipa, worked in St Petersburg for decades and created grand ballets with huge casts. The composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky wrote the music for three of the most famous: *Swan Lake* (1877), *The Sleeping Beauty* (1890) and *The Nutcracker* (1892).

In the early 1900s, a Russian company called the Ballets Russes toured Europe, working with modern painters and composers. Ballet became bold, new and sometimes shocking.

In the United States, Russian-born choreographer George Balanchine co-founded the School of American Ballet in 1934 and later New York City Ballet, creating a fast, sleek American style. *The Nutcracker* became a [[@christmas|Christmas]] tradition across the country, and for many ballet companies it now sells more tickets than any other show.

In India, ballet schools have grown in big cities such as Mumbai, Delhi and Bengaluru, and a few Indian dancers have trained abroad and joined professional companies. Ballet is very different from [[@bharatanatyam|Bharatanatyam]]. Ballet dancers lift away from the floor, reaching up and outward. Bharatanatyam dancers sink into a deep half-sitting stance and strike the ground with their feet. Both, though, take many years of daily practice to master.

Ballet looks light and effortless, but it is one of the most demanding forms of dance. Dancers train their legs, back and core for hours each day, often from childhood. Professional dancers can go through many pairs of pointe shoes in a season, sometimes a pair a performance, because the box softens with sweat and pressure.

text: A statue, or any sculpture, is art you can walk around. Sculptors make them in four main ways.

Carving means cutting material away from a block of [[@stone-carving|stone]] or [[@wood-carving|wood]] until the shape is left. Modelling means building up a soft material, like clay or wax, with your hands. Casting means making a mould and pouring in liquid metal, which hardens into the shape. Assembling means joining pieces together, such as welding steel or fitting parts.
Big statues often use several methods at once. A sculptor might model a small clay version first, then scale it up for carving or casting.

st.prompt: A sculptor carving marble hits a hidden crack and a big piece breaks off the nose. What can they do?

options.t: Very little, because carving only takes material away
Melt the marble and pour it back on
Squash more marble on, like clay

st.reveal: Carving is a one-way process. Once stone is gone, it's gone. That is why carvers study a block carefully before they start, and why clay models are often made first to plan every cut.

d.try: Take a bar of soap and a blunt butter knife or an old spoon, with an adult nearby. Draw a simple shape on the soap, such as a fish or a turtle, then slowly scrape away everything that isn't the shape. You are carving, just like a stone sculptor, only much softer.

Many were painted in bright colours. Scientists have found tiny traces of paint on them, but most of it wore away over the centuries, leaving the bare stone we see in museums.

sec.t:
Carving is the oldest method we know of. People have carved small figures from bone, ivory and stone for tens of thousands of years. Carving is hard and slow. You cannot put material back, so one wrong strike can ruin months of work.

Stone carvers use chisels and hammers. Soft stones like sandstone and marble are easier to shape, while hard [[granite|granite]] takes much longer. That's why the kind of [[@rocks-types|rock]] matters so much.

In Shravanabelagola, Karnataka, the statue of Gommateshwara (also called Bahubali), a figure honoured by Jains, stands about 17 metres tall. It was carved from a single granite rock on a hilltop more than a thousand years ago. Every twelve years, devotees pour milk, [[@turmeric|turmeric]] and flowers over it in a ceremony.

{{story:rocks-types}}

Some of India's most famous early sculpture comes from the time of Emperor [[@ashoka|Ashoka]], more than 2,200 years ago. His craftsmen carved tall stone pillars topped with animals, polished so smooth they still shine.

The best known is the Lion Capital found at Sarnath, near [[@varanasi|Varanasi]]: [[@lions-gir|four lions]] standing back to back. Today it is the national emblem of India, printed on banknotes, [[@passports|passports]] and government papers.

Clay can be pushed, pinched and smoothed, so it's perfect for trying ideas. Many sculptors model a version in clay or wax before making the final work.

Clay can be fired into [[@terracotta|terracotta]], or the model can be used to make a mould for metal. Casting in bronze, a metal made mostly of copper, lets sculptors make strong figures with fine details and thin parts that stone could not support. Chola artists in south India used this method to make dancing gods, as you can read in [[@bronze-casting|How did Chola artists cast bronze gods?]].

Very large statues are usually built more like buildings. The Statue of Liberty in New York has thin copper sheets hammered into shape and fixed to an iron framework inside.

The Statue of Unity in Gujarat, honouring Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, is the tallest statue in the world at 182 metres. That's about twice the height of the Statue of Liberty including its base. It has a frame of steel and concrete, covered with bronze panels.

At Mount Rushmore in South Dakota, USA, four faces of American presidents were carved into a granite mountain between 1927 and 1941. Each is about 18 metres (60 feet) tall. Workers hung from the cliff in harnesses. They used [[@accident-dynamite|dynamite]] to remove most of the rock, then drilled honeycomb patterns of holes and chipped away the rest by hand.

Not everyone celebrates it. The mountain is in the Black Hills, land sacred to the Lakota people, who say it was taken from them. Like many [[@mount-rushmore|monuments]], it means different things to different people.

text: Almost every culture celebrates marriage, but in wildly different ways. In India, a Hindu couple walks around a sacred fire seven times. At a Sikh wedding, the couple circles the holy book four times. In a Muslim nikah, both say they accept the marriage in front of witnesses. In China, red is everywhere, from the bride's dress to the envelopes of money. In Japan, a Shinto couple shares sips of sake. Guests in many countries throw rice, petals or confetti.
Weddings mix religion, family, food and fun. Some are tiny and quiet. Others last for days and feed hundreds of guests.

st.reveal: In Chinese tradition, red stands for luck, joy and protection. Brides often wear a red qipao or embroidered jacket, and envelopes of money are red too. In parts of East Asia, white has long been linked with mourning, though many brides now wear a white gown as well.

myth: The ring goes on the fourth finger because a vein runs straight from it to the heart.
That idea comes from an old Roman belief in a "vein of love". It isn't true. All fingers have similar veins. The custom stuck anyway, and in some countries rings are worn on the right hand instead.

sec.t:
[[@weddings-india|Weddings in India]] can stretch over several days. Before a Hindu or Muslim wedding, the bride's hands and feet are often decorated with [[@mehendi|mehendi]], patterns drawn with henna paste that dries dark orange. Haldi, a turmeric paste, is rubbed on the couple for glowing skin and good luck.

In many north Indian weddings, the groom arrives in a noisy procession called a baraat, sometimes on a white horse, with a brass band and dancing relatives. The main ceremony may happen late at night, at a time chosen as lucky. Sikh couples marry in the morning at a gurdwara, walking around the Guru Granth Sahib as hymns are sung. Guest lists can run into hundreds or even thousands, and teams of cooks stir food in giant pots for days.

Some weddings are loud on purpose. At the end of a Jewish wedding, under a [[canopy|canopy]] called a chuppah, the groom often stamps on a glass wrapped in cloth. Everyone shouts "Mazel tov", meaning good luck. One explanation is that it reminds people of sad times in history, even on a happy day.

In Germany, friends of the couple may gather the night before for Polterabend. They smash old plates and pots, and the couple sweeps up together. It is meant to show they can face a mess as a team.

sec.h: Red for luck, white for brides

sec.t:
At a Shinto wedding in [[@japan-culture|Japan]], the bride and groom take turns sipping sake from three cups of different sizes, three sips from each. The [[ritual|ritual]] is called san-san-kudo, meaning "three, three, nine".

In Mexico and the Philippines, a large looped cord or string of beads called a lazo is often draped around the couple's shoulders, showing they are joined. Many couples there are also given 13 coins, a symbol of sharing everything they own.

In parts of Scotland and Ireland, an old custom called handfasting ties the couple's hands together with ribbon or cloth. Some people link it to the English phrase "tying the knot", though nobody knows for sure where the phrase began.

Some African American couples "jump the broom" at the end of the ceremony, a tradition remembered from the days of slavery, when many enslaved people were not allowed to marry legally. And the strangest part? In many places a wedding is seen as joining two whole families rather than two people, and [[@families-world|family life around the world]] shows how different those families can be.

text: A passport is an official document that proves two things: who you are, and which country you are a citizen of. You show it when you leave your own country and when you arrive in another.

It also carries a polite request. Many passports contain a message from the government asking other countries to let the holder pass safely and to help them if needed. In return, your own country promises to take you back. A passport does not guarantee entry anywhere, though. The country you visit decides whether to let you in, often with a separate permission called a visa.

st.prompt: What is stored on the small chip inside a modern e-passport?

options.t: Your photo and personal details, to check you are the real holder
A GPS tracker that shows where you are at all times
A list of everywhere you have ever been

st.reveal: The chip holds the same information printed on the photo page, including a digital copy of your photo, protected by a digital signature. Border machines read it and compare the photo with your face.

A passport only proves who you are and where you are a citizen. Many countries also require a visa, which is their permission to enter, and border officers can still refuse entry.

sec.t:
Travellers have carried letters of safe passage for thousands of years. A story in the Hebrew Bible tells of a Persian king, around 450 BCE, giving his servant Nehemiah letters asking governors to let him travel to Judah. In [[medieval|medieval]] Europe, kings issued "safe conduct" papers. The word passport probably comes from French words meaning "to pass through a port" or gate.

For a long time, many people crossed borders with no papers at all. That changed during the [[@world-war-one|First World War]], when countries worried about spies and began checking everyone.

In 1920, the League of Nations, a forerunner of the United Nations, held a conference in Paris on passports. It agreed on a standard booklet with a photo, which is roughly what most countries still use.

Today an agency of the UN, the International Civil Aviation Organization, sets the rules so that a passport from India can be read at an [[@airports|airport]] in Brazil or Japan. That is why the bottom of the photo page has two lines of letters, numbers and arrow-like `<<<` marks. Machines can scan them in a second.

Many countries now issue e-passports with a tiny chip and an antenna inside the cover. The chip holds your details and a digital photo, signed with a code that makes forgery very hard. At many [[@airport-security|airports]], automatic gates read the chip and compare the photo with your face using a camera. India issues passports through Passport Seva Kendras, and it has begun issuing chip passports too. Similar ideas about proving identity with data are behind India's [[@aadhaar|Aadhaar]] number.

{{story:aadhaar}}

To get an Indian passport, you apply online, then visit a Passport Seva Kendra with documents proving your identity, address and date of birth. Your photo and [[@fingerprints|fingerprints]] are taken, and police usually check your address before the passport is posted to you. Children need one too, even babies.

Most countries use a few colours for passport covers: dark blue, red, green or black. India's ordinary passport is dark blue. Government officials travelling for work get a white one, and diplomats get a maroon one. The US passport has been blue since 1976.

sec.h: Papers for people without a country
sec.t:
After the First World War and the Russian Revolution, hundreds of thousands of people found themselves with no country willing to give them papers. The Norwegian explorer Fridtjof Nansen, working for the League of Nations, created an identity document for these stateless [[@refugees|refugees]] in 1922, which became known as the Nansen passport. It let them cross borders and look for work. Nansen won the [[@nobel-peace|Nobel Peace Prize]] that year.

Today, [[refugee|refugees]] can receive travel documents under a UN agreement of 1951. For millions of people, the right piece of paper can make the difference between being stuck at a border and starting a new life on the other side.

text: Humans share because, for most of our history, sharing kept us alive. Our ancestors lived in small groups of hunters and gatherers. A hunter might come home empty-handed for days, then catch something far too big to eat alone. Sharing the meat meant everyone ate on good days and bad. Groups that shared survived better than groups that didn't.

Over time, our brains and our cultures came to reward sharing. We feel good when we give, we notice who is generous, and we get angry when someone grabs more than their share. Some of this seems to be with us from a very young age. Parents, friends, religions and traditions build on it.

st.prompt: In a famous game, one player is given money and offers a share to a second player. If the second player says no, neither gets anything. What do many people do when offered a tiny share?

options.t: Say no, so both end up with nothing
Always take it, because something is better than nothing
Ask for the whole amount

st.reveal: Many people turn down very unfair offers, even though it costs them money. It seems we care about fairness enough to pay to punish greed. This is called the ultimatum game, and it has been played in dozens of countries.

n.certNote: Scientists agree that sharing runs deep in humans and starts early. They still debate how much comes from our genes and evolution, and how much is learned from family and culture.

Do they split them evenly, keep more, or give more away? Try it again with an odd number, like seven, and see what they do with the leftover one.
myth: People are naturally selfish, and children only share because adults force them to.

Experiments show very young children help and share without being asked or rewarded. They do become more generous and more focused on fairness as they grow, and family and culture shape that. Selfishness is part of human nature, but so is sharing.
facts: Children start to prefer fair splits

sec.t:
In a well-known experiment in Germany, a researcher "accidentally" dropped a clothes peg in front of toddlers about 18 months old, and reached for it as if he couldn't get it. Most toddlers crawled over and handed it back. They did it without praise or reward. When the researcher threw the peg down on purpose, they didn't bother. Young chimpanzees in the same study helped too, though less often, which suggests the urge to help is old in our family tree.

Children get more choosy as they grow. In a 2008 study in Switzerland, 3- and 4-year-olds mostly kept treats for themselves. By 7 or 8, many more preferred to split things evenly, even giving up a sweet to make it [[@fairness|fair]].

Scientists test sharing with simple money games. In the ultimatum game, one person splits a sum of money with a stranger. If the stranger rejects the offer, neither gets anything. Pure logic says to accept any offer, since a little is better than nothing. Yet around the world, people often reject offers that feel insulting, giving up money to punish greed. Researchers in [[@game-theory|game theory]] have spent decades working out why.

Sharing is also tied to [[@empathy|empathy]], our ability to feel a bit of what someone else feels. Brain scans suggest that giving to others can switch on some of the same reward areas as getting a treat yourself.

Almost every culture has traditions built around sharing food. At the [[@golden-temple|Golden Temple]] in Amritsar, the langar, a free community kitchen, serves meals to tens of thousands of people every day, whatever their religion, caste or wealth. Volunteers chop, cook and wash up side by side.

In the United States, families gather to share a big meal at Thanksgiving, and many towns run food banks. Across India, people share sweets at Diwali and Eid, offer prasad at temples and cook for neighbours at weddings.

Other animals share too, though usually less widely. Chimpanzees sometimes share meat with friends and allies. Vampire bats, which die if they go a couple of nights without blood, regurgitate meals for hungry roost-mates. Humans are unusual for sharing so much with people they barely know, which is one of the things that let us build towns, cities and nations.

text: The US Constitution is the rulebook for how the United States is governed. It was written in 1787 [[@usa-wonder-philadelphia|in Philadelphia]] and starts with the words "We the People".
It splits power into three branches:

- **Congress** makes the laws.
- **The President** carries out the laws.
- **The Supreme Court** decides what the laws mean.

Each branch can check the others, so no one gets too much power. This idea is called *checks and balances*. The President can [[veto|veto]], or block, a law. Congress can overturn a veto with a two-thirds vote. The courts can strike down laws that break the Constitution.

st.reveal: Congress makes laws, the President carries them out, and the courts judge them. Each can check the others. This is called 'checks and balances'.

The Declaration of Independence, from 1776, announced that the colonies were breaking away from Britain. The Constitution, written 11 years later, set up how the new country would be governed.

sec.t:
After the [[@american-revolution|American Revolution]], the 13 former colonies first worked together under a weak agreement called the Articles of Confederation. The central government couldn't collect taxes or settle quarrels between states.

In the summer of 1787, 55 delegates met in Philadelphia, in the building now called Independence Hall. They kept the windows shut so nobody could overhear, despite the heat. [[@george-washington|George Washington]] presided. James Madison, who took careful notes, is often called the Father of the Constitution. On 17 September, 39 delegates signed it.

The Constitution allowed [[@us-civil-war|slavery]] to continue. For counting population, it said each enslaved person would count as three-fifths of a person. Many of the men who signed it owned enslaved people.

It took a civil war to change this. The 13th Amendment ended slavery in 1865. The 14th promised equal protection of the laws, and the 15th said men could not be denied the vote because of race.

The Constitution can be changed by *[[@constitution-amendments|amendments]]*, but it's hard on purpose. An [[amendment|amendment]] needs two-thirds of both houses of Congress and the approval of three-quarters of the states. There have been only 27.

The first ten, added in 1791, are the Bill of Rights: freedoms like free speech and religion. The 19th Amendment gave women the vote in 1920. One amendment, banning alcohol in 1919, was cancelled by another in 1933.

sec.h: The student who finished an amendment
sec.t:
In 1982, a university student in Texas named Gregory Watson wrote a paper about an amendment on how members of Congress are paid. It had been proposed in 1789 but never approved by enough states. He got a C grade.

Watson then wrote letters to state lawmakers for ten years. In 1992, enough states finally approved it, more than 200 years after it was written. It became the 27th Amendment. In 2017, his old university changed his grade to an A.

The US Constitution is short: about 4,400 words originally. [[@constitution|India's Constitution]], which came into force in 1950, is the longest in the world. India's writers studied many countries' [[constitution|constitutions]], including this one, and borrowed ideas such as judicial review and a bill of fundamental rights. The original American parchment is on display at the National Archives in Washington, D.C.

text: An abacus is a frame with rows of beads that slide along rods. Each rod stands for a [[@place-value|place value]]: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands and so on, just like the columns in a number written on paper.

You show a number by sliding beads towards a central bar. To add, you slide more beads in. When a rod fills up past nine, you clear it and move one bead on the next rod to the left. That is exactly what "carrying" means in written addition. Subtraction, multiplication and division work in a similar way, with practice.
The abacus doesn't do the maths for you. It holds the numbers so your mind doesn't have to.

st.prompt: On a Japanese soroban, the top bead on each rod is worth 5 and each lower bead is worth 1. How would you show 7 on one rod?

options.t: Move seven lower beads

st.reveal: Push the 5-bead down and two 1-beads up, and the rod shows 5 + 2 = 7. Each rod can show any digit from 0 to 9 this way. The next rod to the left shows tens, then hundreds, just like place value on paper.

myth: The abacus was invented in China.

sec.t:
The first counting tools were probably pebbles laid in lines drawn in sand or on a board. The word *calculate* comes from the Latin *calculus*, meaning a small pebble.

The oldest surviving counting board is the Salamis tablet, a slab of white marble found on the Greek island of Salamis in 1846. It is about 1.5 metres long and probably more than 2,000 years old. Romans used small bronze hand abacuses with beads in grooves, a bit like a pocket calculator.

Counting boards were common in [[medieval|medieval]] Europe too. They were used to count taxes and trade along busy [[@trade-routes|trade routes]], long before written sums with Indian-style numerals replaced them.

{{story:trade-routes}}

The best-known abacus today is the Chinese *suanpan*. It has a bar across the middle. Each rod has two beads above the bar, worth five each, and five below, worth one each. It was in wide use in China by about the 1500s, and may be older.

Japan adopted the abacus from China and slimmed it down. The modern Japanese *soroban* has one bead above the bar and four below. That is all you need to show every digit from 0 to 9, so there are fewer beads to move and fewer mistakes.

In both countries, shopkeepers, bankers and clerks used the abacus every day for centuries. You can still hear the click of beads in some shops in East Asia.

On 12 November 1946, just after the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], an American army newspaper in Tokyo held a contest. Kiyoshi Matsuzaki, a clerk from the Japanese postal ministry, used a soroban. Private Thomas Nathan Wood of the US Army used an electric calculator, the best machine of the time.

They raced at adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing. Matsuzaki won four of the five rounds. Only in multiplication did the machine come out ahead. [[@calculators|Electronic calculators]] soon became far faster, but for a while the beads were quicker.

In Japan, China, India and many other countries, children learn the abacus in classes after school. After a lot of practice, some learn to picture the abacus in their minds and move the beads in their imagination. In Japanese, this is called *anzan*.

Champions of mental abacus can add long lists of numbers flashed on a screen in a few seconds. Researchers have studied these children to learn how the brain handles pictures and numbers together.

The abacus has also been a tool for blind and partially sighted people. In the 1960s, an American named Tim Cranmer adapted the soroban so that its beads don't slide out of place when touched. The Cranmer abacus is still used to teach maths by touch in many [[@school-history|schools]] for blind students around the world.

Before [[@zero-invent|zero]] was written as a symbol, an empty rod on an abacus already did its job.

text: A watt is a unit of power. It measures how fast [[energy|energy]] is being used or made. A small LED bulb uses about 10 watts. A gigawatt is a billion watts, which in Indian numbers is 100 crore watts.

news.h: India sets a new goal of another 500 gigawatts of clean power in 10 to 11 years
news.t: On 2 November 2026, Prime Minister Narendra Modi opened the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit in New Delhi and announced a target to add another 500 gigawatts (GW) of power capacity from non-fossil sources, such as the Sun, wind, water and nuclear, over the next 10 to 11 years. India already has nearly 300 GW of such capacity, more than half of all its power capacity. He said the sector could attract investment of more than ₹20 lakh crore by the end of the decade. The four-day summit drew participants from over 130 countries. This entry explains what a gigawatt really is.

d.try: Look at the labels on three things at home, like a fan, a phone charger and a fridge, and note their watts. Add them up. Then work out how many homes like yours, with those three things on, would add up to 1 gigawatt. Hint, 1 GW is 100 crore watts.
myth: A gigawatt is an amount of electricity, like a big tank of power.
A gigawatt is a speed, not an amount. It tells you how fast electricity is being made or used. The amount is measured in watt-hours, like the "units" on your electricity bill.
facts: power, how fast energy is used or made

sec.t:
Power units grow in steps of a thousand, a bit like [[@lakh-crore|lakhs and crores]] grow in steps of a hundred.

- 1,000 watts make 1 kilowatt (kW). An air conditioner uses about 1.5 kW.
- 1,000 kilowatts make 1 megawatt (MW). That could run a small town's streetlights.
- 1,000 megawatts make 1 gigawatt (GW). That is the size of a very big power station.

In maths, a billion is 10 to the power 9, written 10⁹. Using [[@exponents|powers of ten]] makes these giant numbers easier to handle.

Now the tricky part. Power is different from energy. Think of water flowing from a tap. Power is how fast the water comes out. Energy is how much water fills your bucket. If a 1 kW heater runs for one hour, it uses 1 kilowatt-hour of energy. That is one "unit" on your electricity bill.

A power plant's "capacity" is the most power it can make at one moment, like a tap fully open. Over a year, real plants make less, because of night, clouds, calm days or repairs.

Inside most power plants, something spins a [[generator|generator]]: steam from burning coal, falling water, or wind pushing giant blades. Solar panels are different, with no moving parts at all. Either way, the plant's gigawatt rating tells you its biggest possible output, not what it makes every hour.

{{story:electricity-made}}

The watt is named after James Watt, a Scottish engineer who greatly improved the steam engine in the 1760s and 1770s. To sell his engines, Watt compared them to horses, and invented the "horsepower". One horsepower is about 746 watts.

In 1882, scientists in Britain agreed to name the unit of electrical power after Watt. In 1960, the watt became part of the international system of [[@measuring-units|measuring units]], used by almost every country.

As power stations grew from small city plants to giant dams and nuclear stations, engineers began talking in megawatts and then gigawatts. Today, countries set their [[climate|climate]] and energy goals in gigawatts.

By mid-2026, India had more than 550 GW of power capacity in total. About 300 GW came from non-fossil sources: [[@solar-india|solar]], wind, hydropower and nuclear. That is more than half, a goal India reached in 2025, five years early.

India also has some of the biggest power projects in the world. The Bhadla solar park in Rajasthan's desert can make more than 2 GW. A [[renewable|renewable]] energy park at Khavda, in Gujarat's Rann of Kutch, is planned to reach 30 GW, bigger than the city of Paris in area. The Tehri dam in Uttarakhand makes about 1 GW from falling water, and each of the two big reactors at Kudankulam in Tamil Nadu is about 1 GW.

On the hottest days, the whole country's demand can climb above 270 GW at once, as millions of fans, coolers and air conditioners switch on.

- 100 crore watts: one gigawatt. About 10 crore LED bulbs of 10 watts each could glow at once.
- More than 550 GW: India's total power capacity in mid-2026. About 300 GW of it is clean, non-fossil power.
- 500 GW more: the extra clean capacity India aims to add over the next 10 to 11 years, announced in November 2026.
- About 20%: how much of its full capacity an Indian solar farm actually produces, on average, across a year. A coal plant can manage far more.
- About 271 GW: India's record demand at a single moment, reached on 21 May 2026 during a heatwave. More homes, cars and factories using electricity will push it higher.

People agree India needs much more electricity. They argue about how to get it.

Supporters of fast solar and wind growth say these are now among the cheapest ways to make power, cut pollution and reduce the money India spends on importing fuel. Others point out that solar and wind are not steady. They say India must also build batteries, [[@energy-storage|energy storage]], stronger power lines and steady sources like hydropower and [[@nuclear-power|nuclear power]], which all cost a lot.

There is also debate over land. Giant solar parks need huge areas, sometimes in deserts used by herders or near wildlife. Some people prefer panels on rooftops, canals and farms, closer to where power is used.

**"A 1 GW plant makes 1 GW all day, every day."** No. That is its top speed. Real output depends on sunlight, wind, water and repairs.

**"Watts and units on the bill are the same."** Watts measure speed. Units, or kilowatt-hours, measure the amount used over time.

**"More gigawatts always means fewer power cuts."** Only if the power can reach homes when it is needed. That needs good wires, storage and planning, not just big plants.

Every switch you flick at home adds a few watts to India's demand. When millions of families switch on air conditioners in summer, those watts add up to gigawatts, and power companies must be ready.

Big clean power targets can mean cleaner air in cities and steadier electricity prices over time, because sunshine and wind cost nothing once panels and [[turbine|turbines]] are built. Most panels are [[photovoltaic|photovoltaic]], turning light straight into electricity.

Try reading your family's electricity bill. Find the units used last month. Then remember: behind each unit is a power plant somewhere, measured in megawatts and gigawatts, and that is [[@electricity-made|where your electricity comes from]].

text: When rain shortens a one-day or T20 cricket match, someone has to decide a fair new target. The Duckworth-Lewis method, now called Duckworth-Lewis-Stern or DLS, does this with maths.

Its big idea is that a batting team has two kinds of resources: the overs it has left and the wickets it still has in hand. At the start of an innings, a team has 100% of its resources. Every over bowled and every wicket lost uses some up. If rain takes some resources away, DLS works out what [[percentage|percentage]] remains and scales the target to match.

st.prompt: In DLS, which loss hurts a batting team's chances more?

options.t: Losing wickets, because each wicket lost cuts its resources
Losing overs, because overs are all that count
Neither, because DLS only looks at the run rate

st.reveal: DLS treats overs and wickets together as resources. A team with 20 overs left and 9 wickets in hand can attack freely. A team with 20 overs and 2 wickets can't, so it has far fewer resources even with the same overs.

sec.h: The match that broke the old rule
sec.t:
Before DLS, [[@cricket-rules|cricket's rules]] for rain were much simpler, and some gave silly results. The most famous came in the 1992 World Cup semi-final in Sydney. South Africa needed 22 runs from 13 balls to beat England. Then it rained.

Under the rule used then, overs lost were simply taken away, starting with England's least productive overs. When play resumed, the scoreboard showed South Africa needing 22 runs from just one ball, which was impossible. Fans booed. The match is often said to have pushed two English statisticians, Frank Duckworth and Tony Lewis, to design something fairer.

Duckworth and Lewis studied hundreds of past matches. They noticed that runs come in a pattern. Teams start carefully, build up and then hit hard at the end, if they still have wickets. Losing early wickets makes teams slow down.

They turned this into a table. Look up the overs left and wickets in hand, and the table gives the percentage of resources still available. For example, a team with all 10 wickets and 50 overs left has 100%. A team with 25 overs left but only 3 wickets has far less than half, because it can't take risks.

To set a target, DLS compares the resources each team had. If the team batting second gets fewer resources because of rain, its target is cut by the same [[@percentages|percentage]]. If the first team was cut short instead, the second team may have to score more than the first team made.

{{story:chance-weather}}

DLS was first used in an international match on New Year's Day 1997, in Harare, Zimbabwe, when the home team beat England. The International Cricket Council made it the standard method in 2001.

Modern cricket got faster, especially after T20 arrived and teams began scoring 300 runs in an ODI regularly. The Australian statistician Steven Stern updated the tables, and in 2014 the method was renamed Duckworth-Lewis-Stern. Today the umpires and scorers use computer software to run it, and a "par score" shows on the screen during rain breaks.

In Kerala, an engineer named V. Jayadevan built a different method, called VJD. It uses its own curves for how teams score and was used in some Indian domestic matches. Supporters say it handles big hitting at the end better. The ICC has stuck with DLS, but the debate shows that there is more than one fair way to split a game.

Cricket fans everywhere still grumble when DLS goes against their team. But a rain rule will never be perfect, because nobody knows what would have happened if the sky had stayed clear. All DLS can do is make a good guess, the same way a forecaster turns cloud patterns into a [[@chance-weather|chance of rain]].

text: The Beatles were four young men from Liverpool, England: John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison and Ringo Starr. Their early songs were short, catchy and full of energy. They were funny in interviews, and their mop-top haircuts and matching suits made them instantly recognisable.

What kept them famous was that they never stood still. In about seven years of recording, they went from simple love songs to albums full of Indian instruments, orchestras and [[@behind-music-recording|studio tricks]] no one had tried before. Many later musicians, from rock bands to [[@film-music-composers|film composers]], say the Beatles showed them what pop music could do.

This was a rumour spread by students and radio DJs in 1969, who claimed to find clues in album covers and songs played backwards. McCartney is alive and still performs concerts today.

sec.t:
Lennon and McCartney met in Liverpool in 1957, when they were teenagers. Harrison joined soon after, and Ringo Starr became the drummer in 1962. Before they were famous, they spent long stretches playing in clubs in Hamburg, Germany, sometimes for hours a night.

That tough training made them a tight band. They learned to keep a crowd dancing, to play through tiredness, and to switch between dozens of songs, including American rock and roll they had heard on imported records. Back home, a record shop manager called Brian Epstein became their manager, and a producer called George Martin signed them to a record label.

By 1963, crowds of screaming fans followed them everywhere in Britain. Newspapers called it "Beatlemania". On 9 February 1964, they appeared on The Ed Sullivan Show in the USA. About 73 million people watched, one of the biggest TV audiences up to that time.

Two months later, Beatles songs filled the top five places on the American singles chart. No one had ever done that before. At concerts, the screaming grew so loud that the band couldn't hear their own instruments. In 1966 they stopped touring altogether.

George Harrison heard Indian music in 1965 and played a sitar on the song "Norwegian Wood". He became a student of the sitar master [[@ravi-shankar|Ravi Shankar]] and travelled to India to learn from him.

In 1968, all four Beatles went to Rishikesh to study meditation with Maharishi Mahesh Yogi. They wrote many songs there, which later appeared on the album often called the White Album. Their interest helped make Indian music, yoga and meditation famous among young people in the West.

The band split up in 1970, after arguments over money, management and music. Each member went on to a solo career. Lennon was killed in New York in 1980, and Harrison died of cancer in 2001.

In 2023, a final Beatles song, "Now and Then", was released. Engineers used computer software to separate Lennon's voice from an old home recording on which a piano was too loud. The song won a Grammy award in 2025, more than half a century after the band broke up.

text: Mindfulness means paying attention to what is happening right now, on purpose, without judging it as good or bad. You might notice your breath going in and out, the feel of your feet on the floor or the sounds in a room.

Most of the time our minds jump around. We replay yesterday or worry about tomorrow. Mindfulness is practice in noticing where your attention has gone and bringing it back. Many adults find it helps them feel calmer and less stressed. You don't need to sit cross-legged or close your eyes. You can be mindful while eating a mango or waiting for a bus.
Does it work? For adults, studies suggest it helps a little, about as much as some other kinds of support. For children in classrooms, the evidence is less clear.

sec.t:
Mindfulness comes from Buddhist meditation, which began in India about 2,500 years ago. The [[@buddha|Buddha]] taught a practice the old Pali language calls *sati*, often translated as mindfulness or awareness. Monks watched their breath, their bodies and their thoughts as a path to understanding the mind.

One tradition, Vipassana, became widely known in modern India through the teacher S. N. Goenka. From the 1970s, his silent ten-day courses spread from a centre at Igatpuri in Maharashtra to many countries. [[@yoga-science|Yoga]] and meditation in Hindu traditions share some of the same ideas, such as close attention to breathing. Jain monks, too, have long practised careful awareness of every action, down to how they walk and eat.

When you feel threatened, your body's alarm system speeds up your heart and breathing. This is the [[@stress|stress]] response. Slow, steady breathing with a long breath out is one of the simplest ways to calm it down, and it is often the first thing mindfulness teaches.

Brain scientists have also studied people who meditate a lot. Some studies report changes in areas linked to attention and emotion. These studies are often small, though, and experts warn against big claims. Mindfulness is best thought of as a skill, like [[@focus|learning to concentrate]], and it gets easier with practice. A few people find that sitting quietly with their thoughts makes them feel worse, not better, and teachers are told to watch for this.

sec.h: A careful look at the evidence
sec.t:
Between 2016 and 2022, researchers at the University of Oxford ran a huge study called MYRIAD. It involved about 85 schools and more than 8,000 pupils aged 11 to 16. Half the schools taught ten mindfulness lessons. The other half carried on as usual.

On average, the mindfulness pupils were no better off a year later. Many didn't practise outside class. The researchers said mindfulness may still help some young people, especially those who choose it themselves. That is a useful reminder: something that helps one person won't always help a whole class, and good science is how we find out.

text: Avul Pakir Jainulabdeen Abdul Kalam was an Indian engineer who helped build the country's rockets and missiles, and then served as India's 11th President from 2002 to 2007. He led the team behind India's first home-built satellite launcher, the SLV-3, which reached [[orbit|orbit]] in 1980.

He is remembered as much for his warmth as for his engineering. He loved talking to schoolchildren, answered thousands of letters, and was often called "the People's President". Many Indians still quote his advice to dream big and work hard.

sec.t:
Kalam was born in 1931 in Rameswaram, a temple town on an island off the coast of Tamil Nadu. His father owned boats and was the imam of a local mosque. The family was not rich, and young Abdul helped by delivering newspapers in the early morning before school.

He was good at maths and curious about flight. He watched seabirds wheel over the shore and wondered how they stayed up. He studied physics at St Joseph's College in Tiruchirappalli, then aerospace engineering at the Madras Institute of Technology. His dream was to be a fighter pilot, but he narrowly missed selection for the [[@indian-air-force|Indian Air Force]].

From the early 1980s Kalam led India's guided missile programme, which built the Prithvi and Agni missiles. This earned him the nickname "Missile Man of India". He was also a key figure in the 1998 nuclear tests at [[@pokhran|Pokhran]]. Many Indians saw this as a proud moment for the country's defence. Others, including people who oppose nuclear weapons, were uneasy that a gentle, much-loved teacher was also a top weapons scientist.

His team also found peaceful uses for their materials. Working with doctors in Hyderabad, they made leg supports, called calipers, for children affected by [[@polio-india|polio]]. The new ones weighed about a tenth of the heavy metal versions, making it far easier for the children to walk. Kalam wrote that this gave him more joy than many of his bigger projects.

In 2002, Kalam was chosen as [[@president-pm|President of India]]. He was the first scientist to hold the job and one of very few Presidents with no background in politics. He opened the gates of Rashtrapati Bhavan to visitors and spent much of his time meeting students across the country. He lived simply, played the [[@veena|veena]] and loved Tamil poetry, especially the ancient book of verses called the [[@thirukkural|Thirukkural]].

After his term, he returned to teaching. On 27 July 2015, while giving a lecture to students at IIM Shillong, he collapsed and died. He was 83. His [[autobiography|autobiography]], Wings of Fire, has sold millions of copies and been translated into many Indian and foreign languages.

text: The Iron Age is the period when iron became the main metal for tools and weapons, taking over from bronze. It began at different times in different places. In West Asia and around the Mediterranean, iron spread widely after about 1200 BCE. In India, iron was in use at least 3,000 years ago, and maybe a lot earlier.

Iron changed the world because its ore is common. Bronze needed tin, which was rare and had to be carried long distances. With iron, almost any community with ore, charcoal and skill could make its own ploughs, [[axis|axes]] and swords. Farming spread into new lands, forests were cleared and kingdoms grew.

sec.h: A metal that is hard to tame
sec.t:
Iron melts at about 1,538 °C, much hotter than the copper used to make [[@bronze-age|bronze]]. Early furnaces couldn't reach that. So smiths learned a different trick. They heated iron ore with charcoal in a clay furnace until it formed a glowing, spongy lump called a bloom. Then they hammered it again and again to squeeze out the waste.

Before people learned this, the only iron they had came from [[meteorite|meteorites]] that fell from space. In 2016, scientists showed that a dagger buried with the Egyptian king Tutankhamun, about 3,300 years ago, was made of meteorite iron.

Near the [[@qutub-minar|Qutub Minar]] in Delhi stands an iron pillar about 7 metres tall and weighing around 6 tonnes. An [[inscription|inscription]] on it is linked to a king named Chandra, thought by most historians to be Chandragupta II of the [[@gupta-golden-age|Gupta]] [[dynasty|dynasty]], about 1,600 years ago.

Iron normally [[@rust|rusts]] when it meets air and water. Yet the pillar has stayed solid. Metallurgists at IIT Kanpur found that its iron contains a lot of phosphorus. Over time this helped a thin, tight protective layer form on the surface, which slows further rusting. The smiths who made it had no idea of this chemistry, but their methods gave just the right result.

Indian smiths also became famous for wootz, a very fine steel. Steel is iron with a small, carefully controlled amount of carbon, which makes it much harder and tougher. Wootz was made by heating iron and plant material in sealed clay pots, then cooling it slowly.

Cakes of wootz from South India and Sri Lanka travelled to the Middle East, where smiths forged them into "Damascus" swords with wavy patterns on the blade. These swords were famous for being strong yet flexible. Ancient Tamil poems mention iron weapons too.

The Hittites of Anatolia, in today's Turkey, were among the early masters of iron. In West Africa, the Nok people of Nigeria smelted iron more than 2,000 years ago. In China, smiths learned to build furnaces hot enough to melt iron and pour it into moulds, making cast iron, by about 500 BCE.

Historians often say the Iron Age ended when written history began in each region. In a way, though, we never left it. Iron, mostly as steel, is still the metal that holds up our bridges, buildings and trains.

text: The Kakatiyas were a [[dynasty|dynasty]] that ruled much of today's Telangana and Andhra Pradesh from about 1163 to 1323. Their capital was Orugallu, meaning "one rock", now Warangal, about 150 kilometres from [[@hyderabad|Hyderabad]].

They are remembered for a strong queen, Rudrama Devi, and for richly carved temples such as the Ramappa temple. They also built hundreds of water tanks that let farmers grow crops through the dry months. The kingdom ended in 1323, when armies of the [[@delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]] captured Warangal.

st.reveal: The Deccan gets most of its rain in a few monsoon months. Kakatiya tanks held that water so farmers could irrigate their fields for the rest of the year. Some, like Ramappa and Pakhal lakes, still store water today.

myth: Women never ruled kingdoms in medieval India.
Rudrama Devi ruled the Kakatiya kingdom for nearly thirty years in the 13th century. Other women, such as Razia Sultan of Delhi, also held the throne.

sec.t:
King Ganapatideva, who ruled for about sixty years, had no son. He chose his daughter Rudrama Devi to succeed him, and she took the throne around 1262.

Some nobles refused to accept a woman as ruler and rebelled, and neighbouring kingdoms attacked. She defeated them and ruled for nearly thirty years. [[inscription|Inscriptions]] often call her by a male title, Rudradeva Maharaja. The traveller [[@marco-polo|Marco Polo]], who visited the east coast of India around the 1290s, described a kingdom ruled by a queen who governed with justice and was loved by her people. Most historians think he meant Rudrama Devi, or the kingdom she had just left to her grandson.

The Deccan plateau gets most of its rain in a few [[monsoon|monsoon]] months, then dries out. The Kakatiyas built a huge network of tanks, artificial lakes held back by earth walls, to catch that rain.

Large ones like Ramappa lake and Pakhal lake were built by kings and generals. Thousands of smaller tanks were built by villages and temples. Water flowed from one tank to the next down gentle slopes, a little like steps. Many still exist, and in 2015 the Telangana government launched a programme named Mission Kakatiya to clean and repair them.

At Warangal, the Kakatiyas built a fort with rings of walls, one inside another: an outer earth wall, then a stone wall with a moat. At its centre stand four carved stone gateways called Kakatiya Kala Thoranam. Each is made of tall pillars topped by a beam carved with swans and flowers.

The gateways are now the emblem of the state of Telangana. A popular story says the Koh-i-Noor diamond was found in mines in Kakatiya lands, near the Krishna river. The mines were real and famous for diamonds, but no record proves the Koh-i-Noor came from them.

In the early 1300s, armies from the Delhi Sultanate attacked Warangal several times. King Prataparudra paid them tribute, but in 1323 an army led by Ulugh Khan, the future Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq, captured the fort. The king was taken prisoner and died soon after.

Some Kakatiya commanders later helped found new kingdoms in the south, and their temples and tanks remained. Each monsoon, rain still fills lakes dug by Kakatiya farmers eight hundred years ago.

text: The American Civil War was fought between the northern and southern states of the USA from 1861 to 1865. Eleven Southern states, where slavery was legal and cotton plantations depended on enslaved workers, broke away and formed the Confederate States of America. The Northern states, called the Union, fought to keep the country together.

After four years and hundreds of thousands of deaths, the Union won. Slavery was abolished across the United States, and about four million enslaved people became free. The war shaped the country so deeply that Americans still argue over how to remember it.
