myth: The Civil War was not really about slavery.

Several Southern states explained why they were leaving the Union in written declarations, and they named protecting slavery as the main reason. Historians agree that slavery was at the heart of the conflict.

sec.t:
By 1860 the United States was growing west, and the big question was whether new states would allow slavery. The North had banned it. The South's [[economy|economy]] relied on it. When [[@abraham-lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]], who opposed spreading slavery, was elected president in 1860, Southern leaders feared slavery's end.

South Carolina left the Union in December 1860, and ten more states followed. In April 1861 Confederate guns fired on Fort Sumter, a Union fort in Charleston harbour. The war had begun.

Both sides expected a short war. It lasted four years. The North had more people, factories and railways. The South had skilful generals, such as Robert E. Lee, and was fighting mostly on its own ground.

New rifles could kill at long range, but generals often still ordered soldiers to charge in lines. Disease killed even more soldiers than bullets. Historians long estimated about 620,000 deaths. A newer study using [[census|census]] records suggests it may have been closer to 750,000.

The battle of Gettysburg in Pennsylvania, in July 1863, was the largest ever fought in North America. That November, Lincoln gave a short speech there that became one of the most quoted in history.

{{story:clothes-cotton}}

On 1 January 1863 Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation declared enslaved people in the rebelling states free. It could only take effect where Union armies reached, but it turned the war into a fight against slavery. Thousands of people escaped to Union lines. [[@harriet-tubman|Harriet Tubman]] guided a Union raid in South Carolina that freed more than 700 people.

About 180,000 Black men served in the Union army, and many more in the navy. Their courage helped persuade many Northerners that Black Americans deserved full citizenship.

Before the war, Britain's huge [[textile|textile]] mills got most of their cotton from the American South. When Union ships blockaded Southern ports, that supply dried up. Mill workers in northern England lost their jobs.

British buyers turned to India. Cotton prices in Bombay shot up, and traders there made fortunes almost overnight. Money poured into new buildings and land reclamation in the city. When the war ended in 1865, prices crashed and many of those fortunes vanished, but the boom left a lasting mark on [[@mumbai|Mumbai]].

General Lee surrendered to General Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox Court House, Virginia, on 9 April 1865. Five days later, Lincoln was shot at a theatre in Washington, D.C., and died the next morning.

The 13th Amendment to the Constitution abolished slavery in December 1865. News of freedom reached enslaved people in Galveston, Texas, only on 19 June 1865. That day, called Juneteenth, became a US national holiday in 2021. Yet for another century, unfair laws in the South kept Black Americans from voting and from equal treatment, until the [[@civil-rights|civil rights movement]] fought to end them.

text: Hawaiian culture grew on a chain of volcanic islands in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, about 3,800 km from the nearest continent. Its people descend from [[@polynesians|Polynesian voyagers]] who arrived by canoe, perhaps about a thousand years ago. Their culture is built around the sea, the land, family and respect for nature.

Today Hawaii is a US state, and its people come from many backgrounds. But Hawaiian traditions, such as hula, the Hawaiian language, [[@sport-surfing|surfing]] and the spirit of aloha, are alive and growing stronger.

st.prompt: In 1976, the canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti. What did its navigator use to find the way?

options.t: Stars, ocean swells, wind and birds, with no instruments
A compass and paper charts
Radio signals from ships

st.reveal: Mau Piailug, a master navigator from Micronesia, guided the canoe about 4,000 km using the rising and setting points of stars, the shape of swells and the flight of seabirds. The voyage helped prove that ancient Polynesians could have found Hawaii on purpose.

n.certNote: Scientists agree Polynesian voyagers were the first people in Hawaii, but they disagree on when they arrived. Estimates range from about 1,700 to about 800 years ago, with many recent studies favouring around 1,000 years ago.

d.try: Read the waves. Fill a tray with water and gently tap one side with a pencil to make ripples. Put a small block in the middle like an island, and tap again. Watch how the ripples bend and bounce around the island. Polynesian navigators could feel similar patterns in the sea and sense land beyond the horizon.
myth: Hula is mainly a dance put on to entertain tourists.

Hula is an old Hawaiian way of keeping history. Its chants and movements tell stories of gods, chiefs, places and families. It is taught in schools called hālau, and serious competitions are held every year.

sec.t:
Hawaiians divided their islands into slices called ahupuaʻa, running from the mountaintops down to the sea. Each slice had forest, farmland and fishing grounds, so a community had everything it needed. Taro, called kalo, was the main crop. Its root was pounded into a paste called poi.

Hawaiians teach that people should care for the land, the ʻāina, because it cares for them. Many of the islands' plants and birds live nowhere else, and some are now [[endangered|endangered]].

Hula is far more than a dance. It tells stories through chant, music and movement, keeping alive history, family lines and legends. There are two main styles: kahiko, the older style performed to chant and drums, and ʻauana, a newer style with guitars and ukuleles. The Merrie Monarch Festival, held every year in Hilo, is one of the world's biggest hula competitions.

The word aloha means hello and goodbye, but also love, kindness and compassion. Many people in Hawaii describe the aloha spirit as a way of treating others.

Surfing was a Hawaiian sport long before anywhere else. Chiefs and ordinary people rode [[@waves-how|waves]] on wooden boards. In the early 1900s, Duke Kahanamoku, a Hawaiian swimmer who won Olympic gold, gave surfing shows in Australia and California that helped spread it worldwide.

In 1810, King Kamehameha I united the islands into one kingdom. In 1893, Queen Liliʻuokalani was overthrown by a group of American businessmen supported by US Marines. Hawaii was annexed by the USA in 1898 and became the 50th state in 1959. In 1993, the [[@congress-usa|US Congress]] formally apologised for the overthrow.

After 1896, schools had to teach in English, and the Hawaiian language almost disappeared. Since the 1980s, Hawaiian-language preschools and schools have brought it back, a model for other [[@endangered-languages|endangered languages]]. Workers from Japan, China, the Philippines, Portugal and Korea also came to work on sugar farms, and their foods and words are part of island life today.

text: The Great Stupa is a huge dome of stone on a hilltop at Sanchi, about 46 kilometres from Bhopal in [[@madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]]. It is one of the oldest stone buildings in India. It was started in the 3rd century BCE by the emperor [[@ashoka|Ashoka]], who became a Buddhist and spread the faith across his [[empire|empire]].

A [[stupa|stupa]] is a Buddhist monument built over relics, the remains of a holy person or objects linked to them. People do not go inside. Instead they walk around it in a circle, clockwise, as a form of prayer. Sanchi's stupa is ringed by a stone railing and four tall carved gateways, called *toranas*, that are among the finest early [[sculpture|sculpture]] in India.

options.t: With symbols, such as an empty throne, a tree or footprints
As a giant golden statue
As a young prince on a horse, in every scene

st.reveal: Early Buddhist artists showed the Buddha's presence through symbols. A Bodhi tree stands for his enlightenment, a wheel for his teaching, footprints for his journeys and an empty throne for the Buddha himself. Statues of the Buddha became common only later.

Archaeological Survey of India, Sanchi.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Sanchi.

myth: The Buddha lived or taught at Sanchi.

There is no record that the Buddha ever visited Sanchi. The stupa was built about two centuries after his death, probably because the hill was close to the rich trading city of Vidisha and had quiet space for monks.

sec.t:
Ashoka's stupa was smaller, made of brick. About a century later, it was enlarged to nearly twice its width and covered in stone. Builders added a railing, a raised walkway and a small stone box on top holding three stacked umbrellas, symbols of honour.

The finished dome is about 36 metres across and 16 metres high. It is shaped like a half-sphere, or [[@shapes-3d|hemisphere]], like an upturned bowl. Some people see it as the dome of the sky over the earth, or as a mountain at the centre of the world.

Around the Great Stupa stand smaller stupas, temples and [[monastery|monasteries]], built over more than a thousand years. One of them, a small flat-roofed shrine known as Temple 17, dates from the Gupta period, around the 5th century CE, and is among the oldest stone temples still standing in India.

Look closely at the gateways and you will notice something missing. The Buddha himself is never carved as a person. Artists showed him through symbols instead: a Bodhi tree, a wheel, his footprints, an empty seat with an umbrella over it.

Historians think early Buddhists felt that a teacher who had gone beyond the cycle of birth and death should not be shown in human form. Statues of the Buddha appeared a few centuries later, in places like Mathura and Gandhara.

Buddhism slowly faded in this part of India, and Sanchi was left alone for centuries. In 1818 a British officer, General Henry Taylor, came across the ruins. Treasure-seekers and amateur diggers soon broke into some stupas looking for gold, causing real damage.

Between 1912 and 1919, the [[archaeologist|archaeologist]] John Marshall led a careful repair and rebuilt fallen gateways. Relics of two of the Buddha's chief disciples, found in a nearby stupa in 1851 and taken to Britain, came back to India and are now kept in a temple at Sanchi.

Today Sanchi is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Great Stupa appears on the back of India's ₹200 note. Buddhist pilgrims from Sri Lanka, Thailand, Japan and elsewhere still walk slowly around it, just as monks did more than 2,000 years ago.

text: Spiti is a high, cold, dry valley in Himachal Pradesh, close to the border with Tibet. Its name is often explained as "the middle land", the land between India and Tibet. Most of it lies above 3,500 metres, among bare brown mountains, deep gorges and a wide river of grey water and stones.

Very little rain falls, because the Himalayan ranges to the south block the [[monsoon|monsoon]]. So Spiti is a cold desert, much like [[@ladakh|Ladakh]]. Only a few thousand families live in its small villages of white mud-brick houses, most of them Buddhist. They farm in the short summer and stay indoors through long, freezing winters.

st.reveal: The great ranges to the south catch the monsoon winds and wring the rain out of them. By the time the air reaches Spiti, it is dry. This "rain shadow" makes Spiti a cold desert, like Ladakh.

sec.h: A sea floor in the sky
sec.t:
The rocks of Spiti were once mud at the bottom of an ancient sea called the Tethys. When India crashed into Asia, that sea floor was squeezed and pushed up to form the [[@himalaya-form|Himalaya]]. [[fossil|Fossils]] came up with it.

Near the village of Langza, at about 4,400 metres, the hillsides are full of fossil shells. Many are [[@ammonites|ammonites]], coiled sea creatures related to squid. Local people sometimes sell them to visitors, though collecting fossils is discouraged so that the sites stay intact for scientists.

Spiti's farming season is short, from about May to September. Villagers grow barley, green peas and potatoes, watering fields with channels fed by melting snow. The peas are prized and sold across north India.

Winters are harsh. Temperatures can fall below −30°C on the coldest nights, and roads are often blocked for days. Families store food, dried dung and wood for months. Children in some villages go to boarding schools lower down during the coldest part of the year.

The air is thin, so visitors are told to take things slowly for the first days. The same thin air makes the night sky dazzling. With almost no lights and very dry air, the Milky Way is easily visible on clear nights.

Spiti is one of the best places in India to try to see a [[@snow-leopard|snow leopard]]. In winter, the big cats follow herds of bharal, or blue sheep, and ibex down towards the valley. Local guides, many of them former herders, now lead small groups of visitors in the snow. The Pin Valley National Park, in a side valley, protects this mountain wildlife.

There are two main ways into Spiti. One road climbs up from Shimla through Kinnaur along the Sutlej and Spiti rivers. The other comes from Manali over the Kunzum Pass, about 4,590 metres high, which is closed by snow for much of the year.

Since 2020, the Atal Tunnel under the Rohtang Pass has made the journey from Manali shorter and safer, though Kunzum still blocks the way in winter. Even so, the trip takes a full day of rough mountain roads, with river crossings, landslides and the odd herd of goats. For many travellers, the long drive is part of the adventure.

text: Chai feels ancient, but it is quite new. In the 1800s, Britain wanted tea it could grow itself instead of buying from China. It set up huge plantations in [[@assam-tea|Assam]] and the hills of Bengal, mostly to sell tea in Britain. Most Indians did not drink it.

In the early 1900s, the tea companies tried to win Indian drinkers too. They gave away cups and set up stalls at stations. Indians took to it, but on their own terms. They boiled the leaves with milk, lots of sugar and spices such as ginger and cardamom. That strong, sweet mix became chai, and today India drinks more tea than almost any country on Earth.

myth: Indians have been drinking chai for thousands of years.

People in parts of Assam drank tea long ago, and some ayurvedic drinks used spices. But milky, sweet chai as a drink for almost everyone only spread in the 20th century, after tea companies pushed it hard.

sec.t:
By 1900, the plantations grew more tea than Britain could drink. So the Indian Tea Association, a group of mostly British planters, turned to India itself. Its teams handed out free tea in cities, at fairs and in mills. Tea stalls popped up on platforms as the [[@indian-railways|railways]] spread, and passengers bought a cup at every stop.

The companies wanted people to brew tea lightly, with a splash of milk. Many Indians ignored this. Street sellers known as chaiwalas boiled cheap tea dust with milk, sugar and spices in one pot. A little tea went a long way that way.

sec.h: The machine that changed the cup
sec.t:
In the 1930s, a planter named William McKercher came up with the CTC method. CTC stands for crush, tear, curl. Leaves pass between metal rollers and come out as hard little grains instead of long leaves.

CTC tea is strong, fast and cheap, and it stands up to boiling in milk. It suited chai perfectly. Today most tea sold in India is CTC. Long, loose leaves like Darjeeling are mostly sold abroad or sipped by tea lovers.

The word itself has a story. In parts of China, tea is called "cha". Places that got tea over land, along trade routes through Central Asia and Persia, kept a word like it: chai in Hindi, Persian and Russian. Places that got tea by sea from Dutch traders, who bought it in a port where people said "te", ended up with "tea", "thé" or "tee".

So when a café in the United States sells a "chai tea", it is really selling tea tea. In the US, "chai" usually means the spiced, milky drink, not plain tea.

India is the world's second-largest tea grower after China, producing about 1.4 billion kilograms in 2023. Most of it is drunk inside India. A small glass of cutting chai, half a full cup, can cost less than a bus ticket.

Every region has its own spin. Kashmir drinks pink noon chai with salt. Hyderabad loves Irani chai with cream. In Kolkata, chai still comes in little clay cups called kulhads, which are thrown away after one use and crumble back into soil. The spices in that cup carry a story of their own, and [[@cardamom-pepper|cardamom]] was once so valued that traders crossed oceans to get it.

text: For most of history, carrots were not orange. The wild carrot is a thin, white, bitter root that still grows along roadsides in Europe and Asia. When people in Central Asia, around what is now Afghanistan and Iran, began farming carrots about 1,100 years ago, the roots were mostly purple and yellow.

Carrots spread west to Europe and east to China and India. Orange carrots became common in the Netherlands in the 1600s. Dutch growers produced sweet, reliable orange varieties, and these spread around the world.

Today orange carrots are so normal that a purple one looks like a trick. In fact it is closer to the original. Purple, yellow, white and red carrots are all still grown, and you can sometimes find bags of mixed "rainbow carrots" in supermarkets in India and the US.

st.prompt: What colour were the first carrots that people grew on farms?

options.t: Purple and yellow
Bright orange
Green

st.reveal: Farmed carrots in Central Asia about 1,100 years ago were mostly purple and yellow. Orange carrots became common in Europe in the 1600s and later spread around the world.

d.try: Grate a little carrot and press it onto a white paper towel. Do the same with beetroot or a purple vegetable if you have one. Compare the stains. The orange one comes from carotene, while purple colours come from a different family of chemicals.
myth: Eating lots of carrots lets you see in the dark.

Carrots give you vitamin A, which healthy eyes need, but extra carrots won't give you night vision. The story was spread in Britain during the Second World War, partly to hide the fact that pilots were using radar.

sec.t:
Orange carrots get their colour from beta-carotene, a [[pigment|pigment]] that also colours mangoes, pumpkins and sweet potatoes. The word carotene comes from the carrot itself. A German chemist, Heinrich Wackenroder, first pulled it out of carrot juice in 1831.

Your body turns beta-carotene into [[vitamin|vitamin]] A, one of the [[@vitamins|vitamins]] your eyes and skin need. Eat a really huge pile of carrots every day and your palms can turn slightly orange. It is called carotenaemia, it is harmless, and it fades when you eat fewer.

Purple carrots get their colour from anthocyanins, the same pigments found in red cabbage and blackberries. Yellow carrots have other carotene-like pigments in smaller amounts.

sec.h: The Dutch and the orange story
sec.t:
There is a popular story that Dutch farmers bred orange carrots to honour William of Orange, the prince who led their fight for independence. It's a lovely tale, but historians have found no clear evidence for it. Orange carrots may simply have been sweeter, grown better in the Dutch [[climate|climate]] and kept well.

What we do know comes partly from art. [[@famous-paintings|Paintings]] of markets and kitchens from the Netherlands in the 1600s show piles of orange carrots. Before then, European pictures more often show purple or yellowish roots.

In 2016 scientists read the carrot's full set of [[gene|genes]]. They found a gene change linked to the build-up of orange colour, and confirmed that carrots were first farmed in Central Asia.

{{story:world-netherlands-water}}

Walk through a North Indian market in winter and you will see carrots that are deep red, not orange. These desi carrots are juicy and sweet, and they are the classic choice for gajar ka halwa. They belong to an Asian group of carrots, separate from the orange European kind.

Some parts of North India also grow black carrots, which are really a very dark purple. They are used to make kanji, a tangy fermented drink that turns a brilliant purple-red. It is often made around Holi, when the weather starts to warm up.

sec.h: The carrot that fooled a war
sec.t:
During [[@world-war-two|the Second World War]], Britain told the public that its pilots could shoot down enemy planes at night because they ate plenty of carrots. Historians think the story helped hide the real secret: a new radar system. It also encouraged people to eat carrots, which were easy to grow while other foods were scarce.

The myth stuck around long after the war. Carrots are good for your eyes in the sense that they help prevent vitamin A shortage, a real cause of night blindness in some parts of the world. But eating more than you need won't sharpen your sight.

And the strangest part? Tiny cells at the back of your eye sort the colours of a carrot from those of a sunset, and you can find out how in [[@eyes-see|how your eyes see]].

text: Wool is the hair of sheep, grown into a thick, curly coat called a fleece. Once a year, usually in spring, a shearer clips the fleece off in one piece, a bit like peeling an orange.

The raw fleece is greasy and full of dirt and bits of grass. It is washed, then combed so the fibres lie in the same direction. Next, the fibres are twisted together into yarn by spinning. Finally, the yarn is knitted into a sweater or woven into a shawl or blanket. Some yarn is dyed bright colours before it is used.

st.reveal: Wool fibres have scales that point one way. Heat, soap and rubbing make the fibres slide past each other and lock, like a ratchet. The fabric pulls tighter and thicker. This is called felting, and people use it on purpose to make felt.

sec.t:
Wool is warm because of its shape. Each fibre is wavy, with a natural bend called crimp. When millions of crimped fibres pile together, they trap tiny pockets of air, and still air is very good at holding in heat.

Wool can also soak up a lot of moisture from sweat or damp air before it starts to feel wet. That is why mountain shepherds and sailors have trusted woollen clothes for centuries, and why a wool blanket still feels cosy in a damp [[@himachal|Shimla]] winter.

A skilled shearer can clip a sheep in a couple of minutes with electric clippers. The fleece comes off in one big piece. It is sorted by quality, since wool from the shoulders is finer than wool from the legs.

Raw wool contains a natural grease called [[lanolin|lanolin]], which keeps rain off the sheep. Washing wool to remove it is called scouring. The lanolin is collected and used in skin creams and lip balms. Then the clean wool is carded, combed between wire brushes, until the fibres form a soft, even web ready for spinning.

In the cold deserts of [[@ladakh|Ladakh]], herders raise Changthangi goats at heights above 4,000 m. In winter, these goats grow an extremely fine, soft undercoat. Collected by combing, it becomes pashmina, the fibre behind famous Kashmiri shawls.

Rajasthan has long been one of India's biggest wool-producing states, though much of its wool is coarse and used for carpets. Shahtoosh, an even finer wool from the Tibetan antelope, is now banned, because hunting for it pushed the antelope towards extinction.

[[@australia|Australia]] and China produce the most wool in the world. Australia is the biggest seller of wool to other countries and leads in fine wool, most of it from Merino sheep. Merinos were first bred in Spain and grow very fine, soft wool.

In the United States, the [[@navajo-nation|Navajo]] people have raised Navajo-Churro sheep for centuries. Navajo weavers use their wool to make rugs and blankets with bold patterns, a craft that is still practised today.

Knitting turns yarn into fabric using loops instead of the over-and-under of [[weaving|weaving]]. That makes knitted wool stretchy, which is perfect for a sweater. A hand-knitted sweater can take a skilled knitter many evenings, and in many Indian and American homes, grandparents still knit for the youngest children every winter.
